{{short description|Continuous mappings can be approximated by ones that are piecewise simple}}

In [[mathematics]], the '''simplicial approximation theorem''' is a foundational result for [[algebraic topology]], guaranteeing that [[continuous mapping]]s can be (by a slight deformation) approximated by ones that are [[piecewise]] of the simplest kind. It applies to mappings between spaces that are built up from [[simplex|simplices]]&mdash;that is, finite [[simplicial complex]]es. The general continuous mapping between such spaces can be represented approximately by the type of mapping that is (''affine''-) linear on each simplex into another simplex, at the cost (i) of sufficient [[barycentric subdivision]] of the simplices of the domain, and (ii) replacement of the actual mapping by a [[homotopic]] one.

This theorem was first proved by [[L.E.J. Brouwer]], by use of the [[Lebesgue covering theorem]] (a result based on [[compactness]]).{{Citation needed|date=August 2023}} It served to put the [[homology theory]] of the time&mdash;the first decade of the twentieth century&mdash;on a rigorous basis, since it showed that the topological effect (on [[homology group]]s) of continuous mappings could in a given case be expressed in a [[finitary]] way. This must be seen against the background of a realisation at the time that continuity was in general compatible with the [[pathological (mathematics)|pathological]], in some other areas. This initiated, one could say, the era of [[combinatorial topology]].

There is a further '''simplicial approximation theorem for homotopies''', stating that a [[homotopy]] between continuous mappings can likewise be approximated by a combinatorial version.

==Statement==

The basic form of the theorem is the following:

{{math_theorem|math_statement=<ref name="Hatcher">{{cite book |last1=Hatcher |first1=Allen |title=Algebraic topology |date=2002 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge; New York |isbn=978-0521795401 |url=https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATpage.html}}{{rp|Theorem 2C.1}}</ref> Let <math>K, L</math> be two [[simplicial complex]]es. If <math>f:|K|\to |L|</math> is a continuous map, then there exists a subdivision <math>K'</math> of <math>K</math> and a [[simplicial map]]ping <math>s: K' \to L</math> whose geometric realization <math>|s|</math> is homotopic to <math>f</math>.

Also, if <math>f</math> is a based map between pointed spaces, then <math>s</math> and the homotopy <math>f \sim |s|</math> can be taken to be based as well.}}

In short, the theorem says any continuous map between simplicial complexes is the geometric realization of a simplicial mapping up to homotopy and subdivision.

Here is a more precise formulation. A simplicial mapping <math>s : K \to L </math> is called a '''simplicial approximation''' of <math> f : |K| \to |L| </math> if for every point <math>x</math> in <math> |K| </math>, <math>|s|(x)</math> belongs to the minimal closed simplex of <math> L </math> containing <math> f(x) </math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Bredon|2013|loc=Definition 22.3.}}</ref>

If <math>s</math> is a simplicial approximation to a map <math> f </math>, then the geometric realization <math>g = |s| </math> of <math>s</math> is necessarily homotopic to <math>f</math>; in fact, the homotopy is given by <math>h_t = (1 - t) f + t g</math>.<ref name="Spanier">{{cite book |last1=Spanier|first1=Edwin H.|title=Algebraic Topology|date=2012|publisher=Springer-Verlag|isbn=9781468493221}}{{rp|Section 3.4, Theorem 3}}</ref>

The simplicial approximation theorem states that given a map <math>f : |K| \to |L| </math>, there exists a [[natural number]] <math> n_0 </math> such that for all <math> n \ge n_0 </math>, there exists a simplicial approximation
:<math> s : \mathrm{Bd}^n K \to L,</math>
to <math>f</math> where <math> \mathrm{Bd}\; K </math> denotes the [[barycentric subdivision]] of <math> K </math>, and <math> \mathrm{Bd}^n K </math> denotes the result of applying barycentric subdivision <math> n </math> times. In fact, the proof of the theorem shows there is a [[real number]] <math>\delta > 0</math> depending on <math>f</math> and <math>L</math> (not just <math>|L|</math>) such that if each simplex in <math>K</math> has diameter less than <math>\delta</math>, then there exists a simplicial approximation to <math>f</math>.

Moreover, if <math>\epsilon:|L|\to\Bbb R</math> is a positive continuous map, then there are subdivisions <math>K',L'</math> of <math>K,L</math> and a simplicial map <math>s: K'\to L'</math> such that <math>g = |s|</math> is <math>\epsilon</math>-homotopic to <math>f</math>; that is, there is a homotopy <math>H:|K|\times[0,1]\to |L|</math> from <math>f</math> to <math>g</math> such that <math>\mathrm{diam}(H(x\times[0,1]))<\epsilon(f(x))</math> for all <math>x\in |K|</math>.{{citation needed|reason=I believe this is true but we should give a citation.|date=November 2025}} So, we may consider the simplicial approximation theorem as a piecewise linear analog of [[Whitney approximation theorem]].

== Applications ==
Here are some typical applications.

:<math>\pi_k S^n = 0, \, k < n.</math>

Indeed, given a map <math>f : S^k \to S^n</math>, it is homotopic to a simplicial map <math>g : S^k \to S^n</math>. Now, for dimension reason, <math>g</math> cannot map onto an ''n''-simplex; i.e., <math>g</math> is not surjective and thus the image lies in a contractible subset and <math>g</math> is homotpic to a constant map. (Strictly speaking, here the based version of the simplicial approximation theorem is used.)

Here is another more substantial but typical application.

:([[Lefschetz fixed point theorem]]) ''For a compact manifold or a finite CW complex <math>X</math>, if the trace of a map <math>f : X \to X</math> (see below) is nonzero, then <math>f</math> admits a fixed point.''

Here, for a field <math>\Lambda</math>, the trace of the map <math>f</math> is the number (an element in <math>\Lambda</math>)
:<math>\operatorname{tr}(f) = \sum_i (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}(f_*|\operatorname{H}_i(X; \Lambda)),</math>
which is a finite number since ''X'' has finite dimension.

''Sketch of proof'':<ref>{{harvnb|Bredon|2013|loc=Proof of Theorem 23.4.}}</ref> We assume <math>f</math> does not have a fixed point and shall show the trace of it is zero.

'''Step 1''': reduces to the case when ''X'' is the geometric realization of a simplicial complex; i.e., <math>X = |K|</math>.

Indeed, ''X'' here is known to be an ENR, a [[Euclidean neighborhood retract]]. Thus, there is a retract <math>r : K \to X</math> from a simplicial complex and <math>f \circ r : K \to X \to X \hookrightarrow K</math> has exactly the same set of fixed points as <math>f</math> does; so we can replace <math>f</math> by <math>f \circ r</math>.

'''Step 2''': <math>\operatorname{tr}(f_*|\operatorname{H}_*(X; \Lambda)) = \operatorname{tr}(f_*|C_*(X; \Lambda)).</math>

This is a linear algebra calculation.

'''Step 3''': subdivide <math>K</math> to <math>K'</math> so that a simplicial approximation <math>g : K' \to K</math> to <math>f</math> exists and note it does not intersect a simplex in the sense below. (We shall write <math>g</math> for both <math>g</math> and the geometric realization of it <math>|g|</math>.)

Since <math>f</math> does not have a fixed point and <math>X</math> is compact, we have <math>\delta = \inf |x - f(x)| > 0</math>. Replacing <math>K</math> by a refinement without loss of generality, we shall assume the diameter of each simplex in <math>K</math> is <math>< \delta/2</math>; note this is not about simplicial approximation.

Let <math>K' \subset K</math> be a subdivision so that the simplicial approximation <math>g : K' \to K</math> exists. Then, by the definition of a simplicial approximation, for each <math>x</math> in <math>X = |K'|</math>, <math>f(x), g(x)</math> belong to the same closed simplex; thus, by the early assumption,
:<math>|f(x) - g(x)| < \delta/2.</math>
It follows:
:<math>|x - g(x)| \ge |x - f(x)| - |f(x) - g(x)| > \delta - \delta/2 = \delta/2.</math>
Thus, for each (closed) simplex <math>\sigma</math> in <math>K</math>,
:<math>g(\sigma) \cap \sigma = \emptyset.</math>

'''Final step'''.

Assuming <math>\Lambda</math> is algebraically closed without loss of generality, the diagonal of the Jordan canonical form of <math>g_*|C_*(X; \Lambda)</math> consists of all zeros. In particular, the trace of it is zero. Then by Step 2 applied to <math>g</math>, we are done since <math>\operatorname{tr}(f) = \operatorname{tr}(g)</math> by the homotopy invariance of homology.

== Proof ==
Source:<ref>{{harvnb|Bredon|2013|loc=Proof of Theorem 22.10.}}</ref>

The idea of the proof is quite intuitive; if there are sufficiently many and sufficiently randomly located vertices, then on each simplex, a continuous map can be approximated by a piecewise-linear map; thus globally so.

Precisely, let <math>\operatorname{St}^0(w)</math> denote the ''open'' [[Star (simplicial complex)|star]] of <math>w</math>; i.e., the union of all relatively-open simplexes containing <math>w</math> in the closure. Note <math>\operatorname{St}^0(w)</math> is the complement of the union of all simplexes disjoint from <math>\operatorname{St}^0(w)</math>; in particular, is an open subset and thus <math>U_w := f^{-1}(\operatorname{St}^0(w))</math>, <math>w</math> vertices, form an open cover of <math>|K|</math>. Let <math>\delta</math> be the [[Lebesgue number]] of this open cover; i.e., a positive real number such that if <math>A \subset |K|</math> is a subset of diameter <math>< \delta</math>, then <math>A</math> is contained in some [[open set]] in the cover.

Now, let <math>K'</math> be some refinement of <math>K</math> with the property that the diameter of each simplex in <math>K'</math> is less than <math>\delta/2</math> (see below for how to find such a refinement). Then the diameter of <math>\operatorname{St}^0(v)</math> is less than <math>\delta</math>, since <math>|x - y| \le |x - v| + |v - y| < \delta</math> for each <math>x, y</math> in <math>\operatorname{St}^0(v)</math>. Thus, for each vertex <math>v</math>, we have <math>\operatorname{St}^0(v) \subset f^{-1}(\operatorname{St}^0(w))</math> or
:<math>f(\operatorname{St}^0(v)) \subset \operatorname{St}^0(w)</math>
for some vertex <math>w</math>. Let <math>s(v)</math> denote some such <math>w</math>. Then <math>s</math> is a map between the sets of the vertices. We note that <math>s</math> extends by linearity to <math>s : K \to L</math>; i.e., it maps simplexes to simplexes <math>\Leftrightarrow</math> for each set of the vertices <math>v_i</math> of a simplex in <math>K</math>, the convex hull <math>\langle s(v_1), \cdots, s(v_r) \rangle</math> is a (closed) simplex in <math>L</math> <math>\Leftrightarrow</math> for each set of the vertices <math>v_i</math> of a simplex in <math>K</math>, there is a relatively-open simplex in <math>L</math> whose closure contains all <math>s(v_i)</math>’s as vertices, possibly with repetition.

Now, the last condition in the above holds since given a set of the vertices <math>v_i</math> of a simplex in <math>K</math>, we have:
:<math>\emptyset \ne f(\cap_i \operatorname{St}^0(v_i)) \subset \cap_i f(\operatorname{St}^0(v_i)) \subset \cap_i \operatorname{St}^0(s(v_i)).</math>
And then we get the (necessary continuous) map <math>g = |s| : |K| \to |L|</math>. Next, for each <math>x</math> in <math>|K|</math>, <math>f(x)</math> belongs to a unique relatively-open simplex <math>\tau</math> in <math>L</math>. Let <math>x = \sum \lambda_i v_i</math> be a [[convex combination]] with nonzero coefficients for some vertices <math>v_i</math> in <math>K.</math> Then <math>g(x) = \sum \lambda_i g(v_i)</math>. Let <math>w_i = g(v_i)</math>. For each <math>i</math>, we have <math>x \in \operatorname{St}^0(v_i)</math> and so
:<math>f(x) \in f(\operatorname{St}^0(v_i)) \subset \operatorname{St}^0(w_i).</math>
Thus, <math>f(x)</math> belongs to some <math>\tau'</math> whose closure contains <math>w_i</math> and by uniqueness, <math>\tau' = \tau</math>. Then we have
:<math>g(x) \in \sum \lambda_i \overline{\tau} \subset \overline{\tau}.</math>
Hence, <math>f(x), g(x)</math> belongs to the same simplex <math>\overline{\tau}</math>. So, if we let <math>h_t = (1 - t) f + g</math>, then <math>h_t</math> is a homotopy <math>f \sim g</math>. <math>\square</math>

Here, we shall give some rigorous argument on how to find a refinement in which the diameter of each simplex is arbitrarily small (of course, this is intuitively entirely obvious.) The argument is by estimating the diameter of a simplex in a barycentric subdivision as follows.

{{math_theorem|name=Lemma|math_statement=Let <math>\sigma</math> be a <math>p</math>-simplex. Then each simplex in the barycentric subdivision of <math>\sigma</math> has diameter <math>\le \frac{p}{p+1}\operatorname{diam}(\sigma)</math>.
Moreover, the estimate is sharp.}}

Since <math>p/(p+1)</math> is less than <math>1</math>, we can make the maximal diameter of a simplex arbitrary small by iterating barycentric subdivisions.

''Proof'':<ref>{{harvnb|Bredon|2013|loc=Proof of Lemma 17.3.}}</ref> By construction, each simplex in the barycentric subdivision has the vertices of the form <math>b(F_0), \cdots</math> for a chain of faces
:<math>\sigma = F_p  \supset \cdots \supset F_0</math>
where <math>F < G</math> means <math>F</math> is a proper face of <math>G</math>, and, thinking <math>F</math> consisting of vertices, the barycenter <math>b(F)</math> of <math>F</math> is
:<math>b(F) = \frac{1}{\# F} \sum_{v \in F} v.</math>
Now, given faces <math>F < G</math>, with <math>g := \# G, f := \#F</math>, we have:
:<math>b(F) - b(G) = \frac{g - f}{g} \left(\frac{1}{f} \sum_{v \in F} v - \frac{1}{g - f}\sum_{v \in G - F} v \right).</math>

Then the expression after <math>\frac{g - f}{g}</math> is in
:<math>\langle v \mid v \in G \rangle + \langle -v \mid v \in G \rangle \subset \langle v - w \mid v, w \in G \rangle</math>
where the bracket means convex hull.
Thus, since <math>(g - f)/g \le (g - 1)/g \le p/(p+1)</math>,
:<math>|b(F) - b(G)| \le \frac{p}{p+1} \max_{v, w \in G} |v - w|.</math>
This implies the diameter of <math>\langle b(F_i) \mid i \rangle</math> is bounded by the claimed bound.

Finally, to see the estimate cannot be improved, first note: for the vertices <math>v_i</math> of <math>\sigma</math>,
:<math>b(\sigma) - v_0 = \frac{1}{p+1}\sum_{i \ge 1} (v_i - v_0).</math>
Thus, for example, if <math>\sigma</math> is the 2-simplex with vertices <math>v_0 = (0, 0), v_1 = (1, 0), v_2 = (1, \epsilon)</math>, then the ratio <math>|b(\sigma) - v_0|/\operatorname{diam}(\sigma)</math> approaches <math>\frac{2}{3}</math> as <math>\epsilon</math> goes to zero. A similar argument works in higher dimension. <math>\square</math>
